answer: Context is the single biggest lever you have — a mediocre ask with great context beats a perfect ask with none. The AI only knows what's in the conversation; it can't see your screen, your files, or your last chat.

What to include:
• The actual material — paste error messages, transcripts, and file contents, don't describe them
• Exact names: systems, versions, file paths, ticket numbers
• What you already tried and what happened
• What done looks like

What to leave out: history that doesn't change the answer, and anything you'd have to say 'ignore that part' about. Lean and specific beats long and vague.

keywords: when should i start a new
answer:
Start a fresh chat when the old context starts hurting more than helping. Signs it's time:
• The assistant keeps referring back to abandoned approaches
• You're correcting the same misunderstanding repeatedly
• The topic has genuinely changed
• Responses get slower, vaguer, or contradict earlier answers

Don't just abandon the chat though — do a handoff first: ask it to summarize objective, current state, decisions made, and next steps into one block, then seed the new chat with it. Ask me to build you a handoff prompt and I'll set it up. 🐾

A handoff moves work to a fresh chat without losing what the old one knew. The flow:
1. Ask the CURRENT chat for a handoff block: objective, current state, decisions made, in-flight work, next steps, gotchas — all in one code block
2. Read it before trusting it — assistants summarize their own work optimistically; fix what's wrong or missing
3. Add exact identifiers the new chat can't guess (paths, versions, URLs)
4. Paste it as the FIRST message of the new chat and ask it to confirm understanding before doing anything
Type something like “make me a handoff prompt” and I'll generate the full template for you.

The prompts that work share four parts:
• GOAL — one sentence a stranger would understand
• CONTEXT — the real material (errors, files, names), pasted not described
• CONSTRAINTS — tools, format, what must NOT change
• DONE — what a good result looks like, measurable if possible

Three habits that beat any template:
1. Plan first — ask the AI to restate the task and propose a plan before doing work; you catch misunderstandings early
2. One task per ask — bundled requests get half-answers
3. Show an example — one example of the output you want beats three paragraphs describing it

That's exactly what I build into every prompt here — describe a task and I'll show you. 🐾

Rule of thumb:
• Codex / Claude Code — hands-on execution: code, scripts, files, repos, testing, anything that touches a machine
• ChatGPT / Claude — thinking and writing: planning, architecture, docs, analysis, drafts
• Both — plan it in ChatGPT/Claude first, then hand the approved plan to Codex/Claude Code to execute
I recommend a destination automatically with every prompt I build — that's the “Send it to” line in my replies.
Plan-first means the AI restates your goal, lists assumptions, asks its questions, and proposes a numbered plan BEFORE doing any work — like plan mode in Codex and Claude Code.

Why it's worth the extra step: misunderstandings get caught when they cost one message, not after 200 lines of wrong code. Every prompt I generate includes a Plan-First module by default; you'll see the AI check in with you before executing.

Treat AI output like work from a fast, confident junior: usually right, occasionally confidently wrong.
• Numbers, names, links, commands — verify against the source before acting
• Code/scripts — run on ONE test target before wide use
• Claims about your environment — the AI can't see it; it's pattern-matching
• Ask “what are you least sure about in that answer?” — surprisingly effective
My prompts bake in a Validation module for exactly this: the AI has to state what it checked before claiming done.
